question: Will a rider typically hear a tire go flat, and how would they usually first notice tire failure?
choice_a: A flat tire is always accompanied by a loud bang that is impossible to miss
choice_b: Tire failure has no noticeable effect on handling
choice_c: You will seldom hear a tire go flat; if the motorcycle starts handling differently, it may be a tire failure
choice_d: Tire failure can only be detected by stopping and visually inspecting the tire
explanation: The manual notes that you will seldom hear a tire go flat -- if the motorcycle starts handling differently, it may be a tire failure, and you must be able to tell from the way the motorcycle reacts.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.33-34, 'Tire Failure'

question: How does the manual say the steering feels if the front tire goes flat?
choice_a: Steering feels lighter and more responsive
choice_b: A front-tire flat has no effect on steering
choice_c: The handlebars will lock in place completely
choice_d: The steering will feel 'heavy,' and the flat is particularly hazardous because it affects steering
explanation: The manual states that if the front tire goes flat, the steering will feel 'heavy,' and a front-wheel flat is particularly hazardous because it affects steering, requiring the rider to steer well to keep balance.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: If either tire goes flat while riding, what does the manual recommend doing first?
choice_a: Hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course
choice_b: Immediately apply both brakes as hard as possible
choice_c: Accelerate to reach the shoulder more quickly
choice_d: Let go of the handgrips to reduce vibration
explanation: The manual instructs that if either tire goes flat while riding, hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course before gradually slowing and pulling to the side of the road.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: If you are sure which tire is flat and braking is required, what does the manual advise about which brake to use?
choice_a: Always apply both brakes at maximum force regardless of which tire is flat
choice_b: Gradually apply the brake of the tire that isn't flat, if you are sure which one it is
choice_c: Never apply either brake once a tire is flat
choice_d: Always apply the brake connected to the flat tire
explanation: The manual advises that if braking is required after a flat, gradually apply the brake of the tire that isn't flat, if you are sure which one that is.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: If the throttle sticks and twisting it back and forth does not free it, what should the rider do?
choice_a: Continue riding normally since the engine will eventually slow on its own
choice_b: Turn off the entire ignition key while still moving at speed
choice_c: Immediately operate the engine cut-off switch and pull in the clutch at the same time
choice_d: Apply the front brake as hard as possible without touching the clutch
explanation: The manual instructs that if a stuck throttle does not free after twisting it back and forth, immediately operate the engine cut-off switch and pull in the clutch at the same time to remove power from the rear wheel.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Stuck Throttle'

question: A 'wobble' is described in the manual as what kind of event?
choice_a: A slow, gradual drift to one side of the lane
choice_b: A sound the engine makes only at idle
choice_c: A vibration that only occurs when the motorcycle is parked
choice_d: The front wheel and handlebars suddenly start to shake from side to side at any speed
explanation: The manual defines a wobble as occurring when the front wheel and handlebars suddenly start to shake from side to side at any speed, and traces most wobbles to improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Wobble'

question: What does the manual warn will happen if you try to 'accelerate out of a wobble'?
choice_a: It will only make the motorcycle more unstable
choice_b: It is the single most effective way to stop a wobble
choice_c: Accelerating has no effect on a wobble either way
choice_d: It will instantly stop the wobble but damage the engine
explanation: The manual explicitly warns that trying to 'accelerate out of a wobble' will only make the motorcycle more unstable.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Wobble'

question: If a wobble occurs, what does the manual say about using the brakes?
choice_a: Apply the front brake hard immediately to stop the wobble
choice_b: Do not apply the brakes; braking could make the wobble worse
choice_c: Apply the rear brake only, as hard as possible
choice_d: Braking is the first and most important response to any wobble
explanation: The manual instructs that during a wobble, a rider should grip the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble, close the throttle gradually, and specifically not apply the brakes, since braking could make the wobble worse.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.34, 'Wobble'

question: What happens if a motorcycle's drive chain or belt breaks while riding?
choice_a: The motorcycle continues to accelerate uncontrollably
choice_b: Nothing changes, since the front wheel is unaffected
choice_c: There is an instant loss of power to the rear wheel; the rider should close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area
choice_d: The rear wheel immediately locks and skids in every case
explanation: The manual explains that a broken chain or belt causes an instant loss of power to the rear wheel; the rider should close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Drive Train Problems'

question: What usually causes an engine to 'lock' or 'freeze,' and what should a rider do about it?
choice_a: It is always caused by using the wrong type of fuel
choice_b: Engine seizure has no relationship to oil level
choice_c: The rider should immediately accelerate to clear the problem
choice_d: It is usually low on oil; the rider should squeeze the clutch to disengage the engine from the rear wheel, pull off, and check the oil
explanation: The manual explains that engine seizure is usually caused by low oil -- the engine's moving parts can't move smoothly and it overheats. The rider should squeeze the clutch to disengage the engine from the rear wheel, pull off the road, and check the oil.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Engine Seizure'

question: If you are riding in traffic and an animal darts into your path, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Remain in your lane -- hitting something small is less dangerous than hitting something big, like a car
choice_b: Always swerve into another lane regardless of traffic
choice_c: Stop completely in your lane no matter what is behind you
choice_d: Accelerate hard to outrun the animal
explanation: The manual advises that if you are in traffic, remain in your lane when an animal is encountered, since hitting something small is less dangerous to you than hitting something big, like a car.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Animals'

question: If you are being chased by a dog, what technique does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Kick at the dog to drive it away
choice_b: Downshift and approach the animal slowly, then accelerate and leave it behind
choice_c: Stop completely and wait for the dog to lose interest
choice_d: Swerve sharply back and forth to confuse the dog
explanation: The manual notes that motorcycles seem to attract dogs, and recommends downshifting and approaching the animal slowly, then accelerating to leave the animal behind -- and never kicking at it.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Animals'

question: For larger animals such as deer, elk, or cattle, what does the manual recommend, and why?
choice_a: Always swerve around them without braking
choice_b: Accelerate past them as quickly as possible
choice_c: Brake and prepare to stop, because they are unpredictable
choice_d: Sound the horn continuously and maintain speed
explanation: The manual advises braking and preparing to stop for larger animals like deer, elk, or cattle, since they are unpredictable.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Animals'

question: If a flying object such as an insect or pebble strikes you while riding, what does the manual say you should do?
choice_a: Immediately let go of the handlebars to inspect your face for injury
choice_b: Brake hard and stop instantly in your lane
choice_c: Remove your helmet to see better
choice_d: Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the handlebars, then pull off the road when safe to repair any damage
explanation: The manual instructs that whatever happens when struck by a flying object, keep your eyes on the road and hands on the handlebars, then pull off the road and repair any damage when it is safe to do so.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Flying Objects'

question: Before turning off the road onto the roadside, what should you check, according to the manual?
choice_a: That the surface of the roadside is firm enough to ride on; if it's soft grass, loose sand, or you're unsure, slow way down before turning onto it
choice_b: Nothing; any roadside surface is safe at any speed
choice_c: Only whether other vehicles are visible in the far distance
choice_d: Only the color of the shoulder pavement
explanation: The manual advises checking the roadside to make sure the surface is firm enough to ride on -- if it is soft grass, loose sand, or you're just not sure about it, slow way down before you turn onto it.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Getting Off the Road'

question: Why does the manual say you should try to get as far off the road as possible when pulling over?
choice_a: Getting far off the road is purely a matter of personal preference with no safety benefit
choice_b: It can be very hard to spot a motorcycle by the side of the road, and you don't want someone else pulling off at the same place
choice_c: State law requires motorcycles to park exactly on the white fog line
choice_d: It is only a concern in urban areas, never on rural roads
explanation: The manual explains that it can be very hard to spot a motorcycle by the side of the road, so you should get as far off the road as you can, since you don't want someone else pulling off at the same place you are.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Getting Off the Road'
